design_detail: Comparison of two English and Welsh sources for 2011–2022 without record linkage (privacy restrictions; called a triangulation approach). ONS: published counts of drug poisoning deaths, by date of occurrence (2024 release of 2023 registrations), in which a specific substance is named in a cause-of-death field, found by ONS natural language processing. NPSUM (National Programme on Substance Use Mortality, King's College London): voluntary coroner reports with the cause of death and the full toxicology report, in which the consulting toxicologist evaluates each detected substance's likely involvement. For each opioid and year, NPSUM opioid-related deaths reported by 1 August 2024 were coded as Code 1 (the opioid named as a cause) or Code 2 (an ambiguous drug-related cause, with the toxicologist implicating the opioid), and the ONS count was divided by the Code 1 share to estimate the total, with 95% confidence intervals from the Wilson score interval for that share. Opioids: heroin/morphine, methadone, tramadol, dihydrocodeine, fentanyl and codeine (paracetamol combinations excluded). Spearman correlations (12 yearly values) of the share missed and of the median number of drugs detected at post-mortem with year and with each other. Short report.
can_establish: What the ONS counts of deaths naming specific opioids would become if, in every year, ONS missed deaths with ambiguous certified causes in the same proportion as NPSUM's coroner-reported cases; how that proportion changed over 2011–2022; and how often NPSUM's opioid-related deaths had several drugs detected at post-mortem.
cannot_establish: The actual number of opioid-related deaths ONS missed (no linkage; the estimate rests on NPSUM cases representing all deaths, which was not tested, and NPSUM held only part of the deaths ONS counted); whether the implicated opioids caused the added deaths (they rest on the consulting toxicologist's judgment of likely involvement, not on the coroner's determination); whether polydrug use caused the ambiguous wording (a correlation between two 12-year trends); or any effect of the undercount on funding, policy or deaths; how many deaths ONS counted under an opioid that a toxicologist would not have implicated (the projection treats every death naming the opioid as correct and can only add deaths, so it measures undercounting only); or whether heroin deaths were recorded as morphine (ONS and the programme both count heroin and morphine as one category, heroin/morphine).

sample.recruitment: Registry data: ONS published counts, from all death registrations in England and Wales, and NPSUM, which receives voluntary reports from over 90% of coroners in England and Wales on deaths related to psychoactive drug use (Methods, p. 2; details in Supplementary Material 2, not read).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: NPSUM opioid-related death: an opioid cited as a cause of death by the coroner (by name, or with the generic terms 'opioid' or 'opiate'), or an ambiguous drug-related cause (e.g. multi-drug toxicity, polydrug use) with the consulting toxicologist implicating the opioid as causative; opioids identified by NPSUM's codes for substances with opioid-receptor agonist activity; deaths from paracetamol–opioid combinations (co-codamol, co-dydramol) excluded to mirror ONS codeine and dihydrocodeine figures; deaths occurring in 2011–2022 and reported by 1 August 2024 (p. 2). ONS: deaths related to drug poisoning naming the substance, by date of occurrence (p. 2); the ICD-10 definition behind the ONS counts is not restated.
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Deaths occurring in 2011–2022 but reported to NPSUM after 1 August 2024 are not included; the effect on the most recent years is not discussed.
sample.selection_effects: NPSUM depends on voluntary reporting; the main text gives the share of coroners reporting (over 90%) but not the share of deaths. In 2011 NPSUM held 416 heroin/morphine deaths, 294 of them with heroin or morphine named as a cause, against 574 such deaths counted by ONS, so NPSUM held about half of the deaths ONS counted if the definitions match (editors' calculation). The authors note that some coroners routinely cite every implicated substance and others do not (p. 4), so the share of ambiguous wording among reporting coroners may not represent all coroners.

exposure.measurement: How a death entered each count, and who decided. The coroner determines the cause(s) of death after evaluating the available evidence (police records, emergency services, pathology, toxicology, GP summaries) (p. 2). ONS counts a death as related to a specific opioid only when the opioid is named in a cause-of-death field on the Record of Inquest, identified by natural language processing; with ambiguous causes such as multi-drug toxicity or polydrug use, ONS cannot tell which substances were involved (pp. 1–2). NPSUM additionally counts a death with an ambiguous cause when the consulting toxicologist implicated the opioid as causative in the toxicology report (p. 2). What was tested: post-mortem toxicology, whose screens are not always comprehensive (p. 4); the share of deaths with toxicology and the panels used are not reported. How deaths certified with only 'opioid' or 'opiate' were coded for specific opioids (Code 1 or Code 2) is not stated.
exposure.polysubstance: 96.8% (16,101 of 16,628) of the NPSUM opioid-related deaths had multiple drugs detected at post-mortem (p. 3). The median number of drugs detected per year appears only in Figure 1 (for heroin/morphine four in 2011 and six in 2022, abstract). Each opioid is reported separately and no all-opioid total is given; how deaths implicating several opioids were counted is not stated.

comparison.controls: ONS counts (named causes only) against NPSUM-based projections for the same years; individual deaths were not linked.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (counts of deaths). Differences between coroner areas in wording, toxicology practice and reporting to NPSUM were not measured.

outcomes.instruments: Yearly ONS counts and estimated totals with 95% confidence intervals by opioid (Table 1); the share missed ('% underestimate', the share of the estimated total not counted by ONS); the median number of drugs detected at post-mortem (Figure 1); Spearman's ρ, labelled very strong (0.70 or more), strong (0.40–0.69), moderate (0.30–0.39), weak (0.20–0.29) or negligible (0.01–0.19).
outcomes.validity_norms: The projection was not validated against linked records.
outcomes.operationalization: Estimated total = ONS count ÷ (1 − NPSUM share of ambiguous-cause cases). '% underestimate' = (estimate − ONS count) ÷ estimate (2011 heroin/morphine: 239 of 813, 29%); relative to the ONS counts, the heroin/morphine estimates are 42% higher in 2011, 57% higher in 2022 and 51% higher over 2011–2022 (editors' calculation).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; no p-values are reported for the 18 Spearman correlations (six opioids, three correlations each), each based on 12 yearly values.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. NPSUM cases were coded by the programme, whose director is the corresponding author.

analysis.effect_sizes: Heroin/morphine: 2011 ONS 574, NPSUM 416 with 122 (29.3%) ambiguous, estimate 813 (95% CI 767–868), 239 additional (193–294); 2022 ONS 1,264, estimate 1,980 (1,894–2,074 in Table 1; 1,895–2,075 in the Results); 2011–2022 ONS 13,471, estimate 20,323 (Table 1 interval 19,382–21,358), 6,852 additional (Results interval 6,557–7,132), 34%. Totals for 2011–2022, ONS against estimate: methadone 5,752 against 9,444 (39%), tramadol 2,455 against 3,865 (36%), dihydrocodeine 1,201 against 1,854 (35%), codeine 1,886 against 2,859 (34%), fentanyl 599 against 887 (32%). Printed Spearman ρ, share missed with year: heroin/morphine 0.78, methadone 0.85, tramadol 0.74, dihydrocodeine 0.43, fentanyl 0.43, codeine 0.43; median drugs with year 0.90, 0.97, 0.97, 0.81, 0.87, 0.94; share missed with median drugs 0.81, 0.79, 0.78, 0.41, 0.33 and, for codeine, 0.59 described as a decrease. Editors' recomputation from Table 1 of ρ for share missed with year: 0.78, 0.85 and 0.74 as printed for heroin/morphine, methadone and tramadol; 0.41 for dihydrocodeine (0.34 to 0.55 allowing for rounding of the estimates); 0.33 for fentanyl (0.31 to 0.34); −0.47 for codeine. With 12 years, ρ of 0.43, 0.41 and 0.33 corresponds to two-sided p of about 0.16, 0.19 and 0.30 (editors' calculation, t approximation).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the study is stated to follow STROBE (Supplementary Material 1, not read); NPSUM was re-confirmed in August 2024 as not requiring research ethics review because all subjects are deceased (p. 2).
analysis.selective_reporting: NPSUM yearly totals and Code 1/Code 2 counts are given only for heroin/morphine in 2011, so the projections cannot be re-derived for other years or opioids; the medians of drugs detected appear only in Figure 1; no sensitivity analysis of the representativeness assumption (for example by coroner area) is reported.
analysis.power: Not reported. Yearly fentanyl counts are small (22–80 ONS deaths), with wide intervals (2012: estimate 41, 28–83).

interpretation_gap.results_show: If ONS misses deaths with ambiguous causes in the same proportion as coroner-reported NPSUM cases, the 13,471 ONS deaths naming heroin or morphine in 2011–2022 correspond to about 20,323 (34% of the estimate missed), with similar shares for the other opioids. For heroin/morphine, methadone and tramadol the share missed rose over the period, as did the median number of drugs detected, and 96.8% of NPSUM opioid-related deaths had several drugs detected. The confidence intervals cover only the sampling variation of NPSUM's ambiguous share, not the assumption that NPSUM represents all deaths.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title says the data 'suggest' systematic underestimation, but the Conclusions say the study 'demonstrates' that ONS underestimated opioid-related deaths for over a decade, 'likely due to coroner reporting practices of polydrug deaths' (p. 5), on the basis of a correlation between two rising 12-year series; the Discussion itself lists other reasons for ambiguous wording (legal sensitivities, simplification for families, a focus on intent) (p. 3). The abstract's 'similar trends' for the other opioids does not hold for codeine, whose share missed fell (Table 1; Figure 1F), and the fentanyl and dihydrocodeine correlations would not be statistically significant (editors' calculation). The statements that the underestimate 'will have led to insufficient resource allocation' and delays in policy (p. 5) and that current resource allocation is almost certainly insufficient (p. 4) are not tested. The claim that the rise in tramadol deaths behind its 2014 scheduling occurred two years earlier (p. 4) is not visible in Table 1, whose estimates rise in the same year as the ONS counts (235 in 2012, 329 in 2013); the 2011 estimate (246) is close to the 2013 ONS count (254), a difference in level, not an earlier rise. The recommendation of drug checking and safe consumption rooms (p. 5) is outside the study's data. The 34% 'underestimate' is the share of the estimate that ONS did not count; relative to the ONS counts the estimate is about 51% higher.

timeline.event: Beynon et al. (card sc_beynon_2007): Liverpool deaths reported as drug-related to a coroner-fed national register (np-SAD) compared across that register's wider definition and narrower official definitions.

Fugelstad et al. (Sweden, online 2017; card sc_fugelstad_2020): death-by-death comparison of certificate-based and toxicology-based counts with an inventory; the certificate-based selection missed about a third of inventory deaths and included about as many deaths the inventory did not count.
Ruhm (card sc_ruhm_2018): US corrections for certificates naming no drug, resting on a similar assumption that deaths without a named drug resemble those with one.
Chief Coroner's Guidance No. 17 on short-form and narrative conclusions (Teague, 2021), cited for how ONS identifies opioid-related deaths from the Record of Inquest.

replication.where_it_stands: A single, unlinked projection by the programme that supplies the correction factor, co-authored by an ONS statistician. Its direction agrees with US studies of certificates naming no drug (cards sc_ruhm_2018, sc_buchanich_2018) and with ONS's own statement, as reported here, that its substance-specific counts are likely underestimates (p. 1). Its size depends on NPSUM's coverage and on whether reporting coroners word their conclusions like other coroners, which only a linkage of ONS and NPSUM records would test. The authors say work on other substances is under way (p. 5).

funding.funder: SC is supported by the China Scholarship Council (Funding, p. 5); no other funding is stated.
funding.declared_conflicts: DM works for the Office for National Statistics. CSC is Director of the National Programme on Substance Use Mortality (Declaration of competing interest, p. 5).
funding.affiliations_note: King's College London, Institute of Pharmaceutical Science (Chen, Copeland); ONS Population Health Monitoring Group (Mais); National Programme on Substance Use Mortality (Copeland). The corresponding author directs the programme whose data provide the correction, and the paper calls for every coronial jurisdiction to report to NPSUM and for sustained NPSUM funding, which it says is not currently available (p. 5). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Record linkage of ONS death registrations with NPSUM case files, or a random sample of coroners' files with toxicology, for the same deaths, reporting for each opioid and year how many ONS deaths without the opioid named had it implicated by the toxicologist, together with NPSUM's coverage by coroner area; and a test of whether ambiguous wording rises with the number of drugs detected within coroner areas, not only across years.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: The ONS frame covers all registered deaths, but the correction factor comes from voluntary NPSUM reports.

NPSUM cases are a non-random set of voluntary coroner reports whose coverage of deaths is not stated in the main text; for heroin/morphine in 2011 NPSUM held about half of the deaths ONS counted (editors' calculation).
16,628 NPSUM opioid-related deaths and 13,471 ONS heroin/morphine deaths; yearly fentanyl numbers are small.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Definitions and data sources are given; no demographics, and NPSUM's yearly totals are not given.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: NPSUM denominators by year and opioid are not reported, and deaths reported after 1 August 2024 are missing for recent years.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Coroners' named causes are standard; the toxicologist's implication of an opioid in ambiguous cases is a reasoned judgment but not validated, and the coding of generic 'opiate' causes is not stated.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Coroners' wording varies, as the authors note, toxicology screens differ, and ONS's language processing and NPSUM's coding are different procedures applied to different sets of deaths.

The intervals ignore the main uncertainty (representativeness); the total intervals disagree between text and table; correlations are printed without signs, some contradict Table 1 and Figure 1, none has a p-value, and correlating two trending 12-year series is read as support for a mechanism.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Reporting to NPSUM is voluntary (over 90% of coroners); the share of deaths reported is not given in the main text.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI-prevalence fits a comparison of two death registers (round brief, certificate studies). The ONS counts are a census of named causes, and the 96.8% of NPSUM opioid-related deaths with several drugs detected is a direct count. The estimates the paper is cited for, however, are projections that assume NPSUM's share of ambiguous-cause deaths applies to all deaths, without linkage, with intervals that exclude that assumption, and with correlation results that are partly irreproducible from the paper's own table; hence high. Citable for: ONS counts deaths as opioid-related only when an opioid is named on the Record of Inquest; in NPSUM's coroner-reported cases, about 29% (2011) to 36% (2022) of heroin/morphine deaths had ambiguous causes with the toxicologist implicating the opioid, so ONS opioid-specific counts are likely to be low; nearly all NPSUM opioid-related deaths had several drugs detected. Not citable for: the true number of opioid deaths in England and Wales (20,323 is a projection), polydrug use as the cause of ambiguous certification, or effects on policy or deaths.

key_findings.finding: ONS context cited by the authors (2023 registrations): 5,448 deaths from drug poisoning in England and Wales (0.94% of all deaths), of which 2,551 (46.8%) were opioid-related; age-standardised opioid-related deaths rose from 22.9 per million in 2012 to 43.8 in 2023.

ONS counts a death as related to a specific opioid only when the opioid is named in a cause-of-death field on the Record of Inquest, using natural language processing; with ambiguous causes such as multi-drug toxicity or polydrug use it cannot determine the substances involved, and ONS acknowledges in its annual reports that its opioid and other substance-specific counts are therefore likely underestimated.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Office for national statistics data (p. 2)

key_findings.finding: NPSUM receives voluntary reports from over 90% of coroners in England and Wales on deaths related to psychoactive drug use, with the coroner's cause of death and the full toxicology report, in which the consulting toxicologist evaluates each detected substance's likely involvement; a death is opioid-related if the coroner cited an opioid (by name or as 'opioid' or 'opiate') or gave an ambiguous drug-related cause while the toxicologist implicated the opioid; paracetamol–opioid combinations were excluded.
key_findings.locator: Methods › National programme on substance use mortality data, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Method: NPSUM deaths for each opioid and year (occurring 2011–2022, reported by 1 August 2024) were split into Code 1 (opioid named as a cause) and Code 2 (ambiguous cause, opioid implicated by the toxicologist), and ONS counts were divided by the Code 1 share (worked example: 123 of 183 named, 67%, so ONS counts are taken to represent 67% of deaths); 95% CIs by the Wilson score interval. Individual deaths could not be linked because of privacy restrictions.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Data analysis, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Heroin/morphine, 2011: ONS identified 574 deaths; NPSUM had 416, of which 122 (29.3%) had ambiguous causes; an estimated 239 additional deaths (95% CI 193–294) gives a total of 813 (767–868), a 29% underestimate. 2022: ONS 1,264, estimate 1,980 (95% CI 1,895–2,075), a 36% underestimate.
key_findings.note: Editors' check: a Wilson interval for 122/416 reproduces 767–868 and 193–294 exactly; 574 ÷ (1 − 122/416) gives 812, not 813. The abstract gives 765–866 for 2011, and Table 1 gives 1,894–2,074 for 2022 (reporting issue 4).

key_findings.finding: Heroin/morphine, 2011–2022: ONS recorded 13,471 deaths; a further 6,852 (95% CI 6,557–7,132) were estimated not counted, giving 20,323, an overall underestimate of 34%.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 2); Table 1; Discussion › Meaning of the study, 1st paragraph (p. 4)
key_findings.note: 'Underestimate' is the share of the estimate that ONS did not count; relative to the ONS count the estimate is 51% higher (editors' calculation). Table 1's interval for the total (19,382–21,358) does not match the Results' interval for the additional deaths (reporting issue 5).

key_findings.finding: Other opioids, 2011–2022 (ONS count against estimate, share missed): methadone 5,752 against 9,444 (39%), tramadol 2,455 against 3,865 (36%), dihydrocodeine 1,201 against 1,854 (35%), codeine 1,886 against 2,859 (34%), fentanyl 599 against 887 (32%).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 2); Table 1, Total and % Underestimate columns (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Yearly share missed, first and last year (editors' calculation from Table 1): heroin/morphine 29.4% to 36.2%; methadone 25.7% to 47.0%; tramadol 32.9% to 44.2%; dihydrocodeine 18.4% to 39.6%; fentanyl 21.1% to 26.8% (13.9% to 46.3% between years); codeine 36.5% to 35.5%, with 49.1% in 2015 and 19.5% in 2021.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation; Figure 1 plots the complementary share captured by ONS, and its codeine panel (F) shows that share rising over time.

key_findings.finding: Printed Spearman correlations: share missed with year, heroin/morphine 0.78, methadone 0.85, tramadol 0.74, dihydrocodeine 0.43, fentanyl 0.43, codeine 0.43; median number of drugs detected with year, 0.90, 0.97, 0.97, 0.81, 0.87 and 0.94; share missed with median drugs, described as a very strong inverse relationship for heroin/morphine (0.81), methadone (0.79) and tramadol (0.78), strong inverse for dihydrocodeine (0.41) and moderate inverse for fentanyl (0.33), while codeine's share missed decreased as the median rose (0.59).
key_findings.note: Signs are not printed, and several values or directions conflict with Table 1 and Figure 1 (reporting issues 1–3). Editors' recomputation from Table 1 and the medians read from Figure 1 reproduces all six median-with-year values and the five 'inverse' values in size (all positive), but gives −0.47 (codeine) and 0.33 (fentanyl) for the share missed with year.

key_findings.finding: 96.8% of the NPSUM opioid-related deaths in the study (16,101 of 16,628) had multiple drugs detected at post-mortem toxicology; for heroin/morphine the median number of drugs detected was four in 2011 and six in 2022.

Reasons the authors give for ambiguous wording: increasing polydrug use (their hypothesis), and also legal sensitivities in deaths involving specific prescription drugs, simplification for bereaved families and the public, and, in intentional or undetermined deaths, a focus on intent or mental health rather than pharmacology.

Limitations stated by the authors: the figures are estimates because the datasets could not be linked and because the share of NPSUM deaths with ambiguous causes is assumed to represent all drug deaths, which coroners' differing practices could bias; toxicology screens are not always comprehensive, so polydrug use and the median number of drugs may be underestimated.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Strengths and weaknesses of this and other studies, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Recommendations: coroners should list every drug implicated, so that ONS processing recognises each substance; every coronial jurisdiction should report to NPSUM, which would need sustained funding that is not currently available; adopting ICD-11, with more detailed drug-poisoning codes, could improve ONS data.

reporting_issues.issue: Correlation coefficients are printed without signs, and the relationships between the share missed and the median number of drugs detected are called inverse for heroin/morphine, methadone, tramadol, dihydrocodeine and fentanyl, although the share missed and the median both rose. Recomputed from Table 1 and the yearly medians read from Figure 1, these five coefficients reproduce the printed sizes and are all positive (0.81, 0.79, 0.78, 0.39 and 0.33), while codeine's is negative (−0.59, printed 0.59) (editors' calculation; the medians read from the figure also reproduce every printed correlation of the median with year).
reporting_issues.consequence: For five opioids the relationship is positive (more drugs detected, larger share missed), as the abstract implies; the word inverse in the Results should be disregarded and only codeine's relationship read as negative.

reporting_issues.issue: The coefficients printed for the share missed over time do not all fit Table 1: recomputed from it, codeine's is −0.47 (the share missed fell, as Figure 1F shows), not 0.43 within 'increased rates of these underestimations', and fentanyl's is 0.33 (0.31 to 0.34 allowing for rounding of the estimates), not 0.43 (editors' calculation). As printed, the codeine coefficients cannot all hold: if both the share missed and the median rose over time (0.43 and 0.94), their correlation with each other could not be −0.59 (editors' check: the matrix is not a valid correlation matrix).
reporting_issues.consequence: Codeine does not show the rising undercount the abstract attributes to 'similar trends'; cite Table 1's yearly counts rather than the printed coefficients for codeine and fentanyl.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say the correlations were computed to see if there were any significant relationships, but no p-values or intervals are given; with 12 years, coefficients of 0.43, 0.41 and 0.33 correspond to two-sided p of about 0.16, 0.19 and 0.30 (editors' calculation), yet they are labelled strong or moderate.
reporting_issues.consequence: Only the heroin/morphine, methadone and tramadol trends are clearly distinguishable from chance; correlations between two series that both trend over time do not show that one drives the other.

reporting_issues.issue: Intervals for the same estimate differ between places: 2011 heroin/morphine 765–866 in the abstract against 767–868 in the Results and Table 1 (the latter reproduces as a Wilson interval for 122/416, editors' check); 2022, 1,894–2,074 in the abstract and Table 1 against 1,895–2,075 in the Results. The 2011 point estimate (813) is 812 when recomputed from 574 and 122/416 (editors' calculation).

For heroin/morphine over 2011–2022, the Results give 6,852 additional deaths with a 95% CI of 6,557–7,132, implying a total of 20,028–20,603, while Table 1 gives 20,323 (19,382–21,358). The Table 1 limits equal the sums of the yearly limits (with 2015's upper limit taken as about 1,803; issue 6) (editors' check), an interval that assumes all yearly errors move together.
reporting_issues.consequence: Two different intervals are given for the same quantity, and neither reflects the main uncertainty (whether NPSUM cases are representative); present 20,323 as a projection without a precise interval.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints the 2015 heroin/morphine interval as 1,657–2,803 around an estimate of 1,727, an upper limit far out of line with the other years; about 1,803 makes the yearly upper limits add up to the printed total's 21,358 (editors' check). The 2020 methadone interval is printed as '(; 1128–1290)'.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical errors; the 2015 upper limit should be read as about 1,803.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes the median number of 'co-administered' drugs, while the Methods measure drugs detected at post-mortem.
reporting_issues.consequence: Detection does not show that the drugs were taken together; describe the figure as drugs detected.
